theme: Christian freedom; idolatry; love limits liberty
readingInstruction: Read 1 Corinthians 8:1-10:33. These three chapters answer a question about food offered to idols. Read for the principle: how do Christians use their freedom? Notice Paul’s own example in chapter 9, the warning from Israel in chapter 10, and the closing command in 10:31.
settingTheScene: Much of the meat sold in Corinth had first been offered to idols in pagan temples. Some believers said that since idols are nothing, eating that meat was fine. Others, who had been idol worshipers, felt that eating it was a return to idolatry. Paul does not simply side with the strong. He offers principles of knowledge, love, freedom, and warning that apply well beyond food. Typical situations today include entertainment, drinking, holidays, and cultural practices.
observation: “This knowledge puffs up, but love builds up” (8:1).
“Yet for us there is one God, the Father, from whom are all things and for whom we exist, and one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom are all things and through whom we exist” (8:6).
“For though I am free from all, I have made myself a servant to all, that I might win more of them” (9:19).
“I have become all things to all people, that by all means I might save some” (9:22).
“And all drank the same spiritual drink. For they were drinking from the spiritual Rock that followed them, and the Rock was Christ” (10:4).
“Now these things happened to them as an example, but they were written down for our instruction, on whom the end of the ages has come” (10:11).
“God is faithful, and he will not let you be tempted beyond your ability” (10:13).
“So, whether you eat or drink, or whatever you do, do all to the glory of God” (10:31).
interpretation:
Paul starts with a general principle: “Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up.” It is possible to be right and unloving. He agrees with the strong in doctrine: “An idol has no real existence, and there is no God but one.” The great confession of 8:6 echoes the Shema: “For us there is one God, the Father… and one Lord, Jesus Christ.” Paul places Jesus within the identity of the one God. Yet not everyone has this knowledge, and a weaker conscience may be defiled. “Take care that this right of yours does not somehow become a stumbling block to the weak.” Love limits liberty: “If food is a cause of my brother’s stumbling, I will never eat meat, lest I cause my brother to stumble.”

In chapter 9, Paul uses himself as an example. He is an apostle with rights: to eat and drink, to be married, to be supported by the churches, as the Lord commanded that those who proclaim the gospel get their living by the gospel. “But I have made no use of any of these rights.” He renounces them to avoid putting an obstacle in the way of the gospel. “For though I am free from all, I have made myself a servant to all, that I might win more of them.” To the Jews he became as a Jew; to those under the law as under the law; to those outside the law as outside the law, though not outside the law of God; to the weak, weak. “I have become all things to all people, that by all means I might save some. I do it all for the sake of the gospel.” Paul adapts his behavior, not his message. Then he compares the Christian life to a race and to boxing, with self-discipline and an imperishable crown.

Chapter 10 warns from Israel’s history. All were baptized into Moses in the cloud and the sea, all ate the same spiritual food and drank the same spiritual drink, “for they were drinking from the spiritual Rock that followed them, and the Rock was Christ.” Yet with most of them God was not pleased, and they were overthrown in the wilderness. Idolatry, immorality, testing the Lord, and grumbling brought judgment. “These things happened to them as an example, but they were written down for our instruction, on whom the end of the ages has come. Therefore let anyone who thinks that he stands take heed lest he fall.” This is a key text for reading the Old Testament as Christian Scripture: Christ was present in Israel’s story, and its lessons are for us.

And then comfort: “No temptation has overtaken you that is not common to man. God is faithful, and he will not let you be tempted beyond your ability, but with the temptation he will also provide the way of escape, that you may be able to endure it.” The instruction is to flee idolatry. The Lord’s Supper is a participation in the blood and body of Christ, and one cannot partake of the table of the Lord and the table of demons.

The closing principles in 10:23 to 11:1: not everything is helpful, seek the good of your neighbor, give thanks, and avoid causing offense. “So, whether you eat or drink, or whatever you do, do all to the glory of God.” Give no offense to Jews, Greeks, or the church of God. “Be imitators of me, as I am of Christ.”
connection: Deuteronomy 6:4 is the Shema, which Paul reworks in 8:6. Numbers 11, 14, 16, 21, and 25 describe the wilderness failures. Exodus 14 and 17 describe the sea and the rock. Romans 14 to 15 treats a similar question. Acts 15:28-29 and Revelation 2:14, 20 address meat offered to idols. Philippians 3:12-14 and 2 Timothy 4:7 speak of the race. Hebrews 3 to 4 also draw lessons from Israel’s wilderness. John 4:34 and Colossians 3:17 speak of doing all for God.
application:
Name a freedom you have that might hinder a friend or new believer. Be willing to give it up for love.

Ask yourself: Does my knowledge puff me up or build up others?

Do one ordinary thing today, eating or working, “to the glory of God” and say so in your heart.
prayerPrompts: Thank God for the one God and one Lord.
Ask him to keep your knowledge from puffing you up and make you loving.
Ask him to help you give up a liberty if it would help a brother or sister.
